title: Windows Built-in Administrators Membership Changes
exclusions: Detects successful Windows Security events 4732 and 4733 for the built-in local Administrators group SID `S-1-5-32-544` on covered Windows computers. It does not detect failed attempts, group creation or deletion, changes to other privileged groups, direct assignment of user rights, token use, domain-group membership changed on a domain controller, directory replication history, Linux/macOS privilege changes, or a current-state membership drift without a retained event. A 4733 removal can reduce privilege and is not inherently malicious; this UC reports it for review. Event 4735 is not used as proof of membership because Microsoft documents that it commonly precedes 4732/4733 without naming the member. The `index=windows` value is a deployment choice. No exception may erase the base event; approved changes may suppress notification only after exact host, member SID, actor SID, action, ticket, and bounded time checks. This documentation-only review does not attest that auditing, forwarding, field extraction, alerting, or response works in production.
evidence: Retain the effective Audit Security Group Management policy; covered-host inventory; Windows event-subscription and Splunk input configuration; Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows version; raw 4732/4733 XML; `windows_builtin_administrators_membership_changes` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and results; approved-change lookup revisions; alert-action history; incident dispositions; and dated positive, negative, boundary, duplicate-delivery, unresolved-SID, late-arrival, and suppression tests. Each finding must preserve host, event time, channel, provider, event code, event record ID where available, actor SID/name/domain/logon ID, member SID/name, target group SID/name/domain, action, source, source type, index time, and matched change ticket. This documentation review created no runtime or SME-sign-off evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest one Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing event 4732 from `host=win-lab-01`, Security channel, with `TargetSid=S-1-5-32-544`, `MemberSid=S-1-5-21-100-200-300-1107`, `MemberName=-`, `SubjectUserSid=S-1-5-21-100-200-300-1500`, `SubjectUserName=change.operator`, and `SubjectLogonId=0x44a1`; expect exactly one row with `action=added`. Ingest a corresponding 4733 with a distinct record ID and expect exactly one `removed` row. Verify the unresolved member name remains `-` while the SID remains actionable.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for: event 4732 targeting `S-1-5-32-545` (Users), event 4728 adding a domain-global-group member, event 4735 with no membership payload, event 4732 from the Application channel, and event 4732 missing `TargetSid`. An approved-change fixture may suppress notification only when exact host, member SID, actor SID, action, inclusive start, exclusive expiry, and ticket all match; the unsuppressed base-search result and raw event must still remain available.

dataSources: Primary source: the Windows Security event channel from every governed workstation and member server, collected in XML or classic rendering with the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows. Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing events 4732 and 4733 are success events emitted once per member added to or removed from a security-enabled local group when Audit Security Group Management success auditing is effective. Required source fields are `EventCode`, `TargetSid`, `TargetUserName`, `TargetDomainName`, `MemberSid`, `MemberName`, `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, and `SubjectLogonId`; retain `EventRecordID`, `Computer`, `Channel`, and `Provider_Name` when available. Splunk distinguishes classic `WinEventLog` and XML `XmlWinEventLog` source types and source values such as `WinEventLog:Security` and `XmlWinEventLog:Security`.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for supported Windows event collection, extraction, and CIM knowledge. A deployment-owned security-content app should hold the saved search, covered-host inventory, exact approved-change lookup, dashboard, tests, and response runbook.
spl:
index=windows source IN ("WinEventLog:Security","XmlWinEventLog:Security") sourcetype IN ("WinEventLog","XmlWinEventLog") EventCode IN (4732,4733) TargetSid="S-1-5-32-544"
| eval action=case(EventCode=4732,"added",EventCode=4733,"removed"), actor=coalesce(SubjectDomainName."\\".SubjectUserName,SubjectUserName,SubjectUserSid), member=if(isnotnull(MemberName) AND MemberName!="-",MemberName,MemberSid), group=coalesce(TargetDomainName."\\".TargetUserName,TargetUserName,TargetSid)
| where isnotnull(action) AND len(MemberSid)>0 AND len(SubjectUserSid)>0
| table _time host action actor SubjectUserSid SubjectUserName SubjectDomainName SubjectLogonId member MemberSid MemberName group TargetSid TargetUserName TargetDomainName EventCode EventRecordID Provider_Name source sourcetype _indextime
| sort 0 - _time host EventRecordID
description: Reports one review row for each retained Windows 4732 addition to or 4733 removal from the built-in local Administrators group, identified by language-independent SID `S-1-5-32-544`. The row grain is the Windows audit event and includes the initiating security principal, changed member SID, target computer, direction of change, and event identity; there is no count threshold.
value: Local Administrators membership grants broad control over a Windows computer. Prompt, attributable review of every addition exposes unauthorized privilege escalation or persistence, while review of removals catches accidental loss of required administrative access and preserves a defensible change trail without treating a localized group name as identity. This shortens the interval between an unexplained privilege grant and accountable review or removal.
implementation: Enable Audit Security Group Management success auditing on the covered Windows computers, collect the Security channel in a qualified classic or XML format, and verify the documented 4732/4733 fields. Save the SPL as `windows_builtin_administrators_membership_changes`, run it every five minutes over a measured overlap, and alert on additions by default while routing removals for change review. Use the built-in group SID rather than the localized `Administrators` name; enrich and suppress notification only through an exact, expiring approved-change record.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — Local Administrators Change Review`: show collection coverage and audit-policy health before detections; additions and removals by host, actor, member SID, and business owner; unresolved member SIDs; changes without a matching ticket; repeated add/remove sequences; and event-ingest delay. The drilldown table must expose raw 4732/4733 XML, event record ID, actor logon ID, host inventory, approved-change match, nearby 4624/4648 session evidence where retained, and incident disposition. Never render missing Security events as proof of unchanged membership.
schema: Microsoft Windows Security event schema with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows search-time fields
dataModelAcceleration: The Splunk Add-on documents 4732/4733 mappings to Change datasets, with coverage differing by classic/XML source and add-on release. Validate `Change.Account_Management` or `Change.Endpoint_Changes` tags and normalized fields against the installed add-on before using acceleration. The primary search intentionally uses Microsoft event fields because `TargetSid`, `MemberSid`, actor SID/logon ID, and event record identity are required; a generic `tstats count` is not equivalent.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row is a real audited membership change, but authorization and risk require context.

1. **Endpoint provisioning or domain join** — A build platform may add a governed support group to local Administrators. Require exact build workflow ID, target host, member SID, automation actor SID, and short enrollment window; compare the resulting membership with the approved baseline.

2. **Privileged-access management activation** — A JIT/PAM workflow may add a temporary support principal and later remove it. Confirm the PAM request, approver, actor identity, endpoint, start/expiry, and paired 4732/4733 events. An addition without timely removal remains actionable.

3. **Software deployment or support tooling** — An installer, EDR platform, inventory agent, or remote-support product may add a service account or group. Verify vendor deployment documentation, package/job ID, code signature, exact member SID, and whether permanent local administration is actually required.

4. **Break-glass or incident response** — Responders may grant emergency local administration. Correlate incident ID, commander approval, named user, affected host, start, expiry, and post-incident removal. Emergency status changes severity; it does not justify deleting evidence.

5. **Group Policy, MDM, Desired State Configuration, or baseline remediation** — Policy can repeatedly reconcile local group membership after drift. Confirm the responsible policy object/profile, revision, deployment ring, expected SID set, and management-system audit. Repeated add/remove oscillation can indicate conflicting policies and should not be silently suppressed.

6. **Manual approved maintenance** — A server or endpoint owner may grant temporary access through Computer Management, PowerShell, or `net localgroup`. Require a ticket that names exact host, member SID, actor SID, action, purpose, approved start, exclusive expiry, and removal owner.

7. **Account or group migration** — SID-history, domain migration, service-account replacement, or renamed groups can produce expected replacement changes. Resolve SIDs against authoritative identity records, preserve old/new membership, and verify that obsolete privilege is removed.

8. **Removal events** — Event 4733 often represents safe cleanup, policy enforcement, account retirement, or access revocation. Route it as auditable change unless the removed member is required for recovery/service operation or the removal follows a suspicious short-lived addition.

**Safe suppression:** apply notification suppression only after the base result using an exact lookup key of `host,MemberSid,SubjectUserSid,action` plus numeric inclusive start and exclusive expiry, ticket, owner, approver, and reason. Reject wildcards, group-name-only keys, actor-name-only keys, open-ended records, and any suppression of collection/audit-policy health. Preserve matched and unmatched events in the review trail.
hardware: Windows workstations and member servers whose Security channel and local built-in Administrators group are governed. Domain controllers also emit 4732/4733 for domain-local groups, but this detector restricts identity to built-in SID S-1-5-32-544 and does not replace dedicated domain privileged-group monitoring.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft 4732/4733 event, Advanced Audit Policy, and SID documentation; MITRE ATT&CK T1098.007 and DET0310; and Splunk Microsoft Windows add-on source-type/CIM documentation; audit policy, event generation, collection, extraction, SPL, fixtures, suppression, alerting, dashboard, and response were specified but not executed or Windows/security/Splunk-SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: Security Group Management event volume is documented as low. The scheduled search scans two event codes over a bounded interval and performs no unbounded join or transaction; retention volume depends on endpoint count and administrative-change rate.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and identity contract

Assign Windows endpoint/server, identity, privileged-access, Splunk data, detection, and incident owners. Inventory the computers in scope and record stable host identity, owner, environment, administrative tier, expected local Administrators member SIDs, and enrollment/retirement times. Use the well-known group SID `S-1-5-32-544` as the detector identity. Do not filter on the localized display name `Administrators`, and do not infer membership from Event 4735.

Microsoft documents 4732 as one success event for each member added to a security-enabled local group and 4733 as one for each member removed. Both can occur on workstations, member servers, and domain controllers. The event identifies the subject that performed the operation, the member, and the target group. `MemberName` may be `-`, especially for a local-group operation involving a domain principal, so `MemberSid` is mandatory and is never replaced with `unknown`. A 4732 proves that Windows audited an addition; it does not prove malicious intent, interactive origin, or that the member later used privilege. A 4733 proves removal and is retained even when it is benign cleanup.

## Step 1 — Enable and verify Windows auditing

Configure **Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Account Management > Audit Security Group Management** for Success through the governed policy mechanism. Microsoft states this subcategory has no failure events. Avoid a conflicting legacy/advanced audit-policy configuration. On representative systems, record effective policy with `auditpol /get /subcategory:"Security Group Management"`, policy source/resultant set, OS build, locale, channel size/retention, and last policy refresh.

Generate changes only in an isolated lab or approved disposable local account/group workflow. Add a test member to the built-in Administrators group and remove it. In Event Viewer, inspect **Windows Logs > Security** and export raw XML. Verify provider `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing`, channel `Security`, IDs 4732 and 4733, target SID `S-1-5-32-544`, member SID, subject SID/name/domain/logon ID, computer, event time, and event record ID. Restore baseline membership immediately. Never add an uncontrolled account to production Administrators merely to test monitoring.

Audit-policy health is a separate control. Detect covered hosts that stop sending Security events or whose effective policy drifts. Missing 4732/4733 events are not evidence that membership did not change. Periodically compare current local Administrators membership from a governed endpoint-management inventory with the approved SID baseline; that state control can catch changes made while auditing or forwarding was unavailable.

## Step 2 — Collect and normalize the Security channel

Use the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows and a least-privilege Universal Forwarder, Windows Event Collector subscription, or other supported Windows input. Qualify either classic or XML rendering and keep it consistent enough to test field extraction. Splunk documents `WinEventLog` for classic channels and `XmlWinEventLog` for XML channels in add-on 5.0.0 and later, with source distinguishing the Security channel. The catalogue SPL accepts both source/type forms but teams may narrow it to their qualified format.

Place deployment-specific input settings in `local` or a separate deployment app, not the add-on's `default` directory. Route the Security channel to the local `windows` index or replace that explicit index in the SPL with the deployment's RBAC-approved security index. Treat index naming as local configuration, not a Splunk default. Preserve raw XML where possible and protect Security data because it contains account identifiers and administrative activity.

Verify on each supported rendering that search-time fields exactly match `EventCode`, `TargetSid`, `TargetUserName`, `TargetDomainName`, `MemberSid`, `MemberName`, `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, and `SubjectLogonId`. Record aliases only after inspecting raw events. Verify source, source type, host/computer mapping, provider, channel, event record ID, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Do not create a field default that converts a missing SID to the Administrators SID or resolves `-` to an arbitrary account.

## Step 3 — Establish source and duplicate-delivery health

Build a coverage search keyed by stable computer inventory. Report a host that has no expected Security heartbeat, forwarding lag above the measured service objective, channel overwrite/drop evidence, disabled input, malformed XML, unexpected source/type, missing required SID fields, or audit-policy drift. Keep source-health findings separate from membership results so missing data cannot render a dashboard green.

Windows Event Forwarding, forwarder cloning, or overlapping subscriptions can duplicate the same event. Measure duplicates by stable computer plus channel plus event record ID and provider. If the deployment proves those fields stable, suppress duplicate notification while retaining each raw copy and recording transport paths. Do not use `dedup host MemberSid EventCode` because two legitimate changes to the same membership would collapse. A record-ID reset after log clear/reinstall must be handled with channel creation/log-clear context and time, not silently discarded.

Measure p99 indexing delay. Schedule the saved search every five minutes with an overlap large enough to include late events, then maintain a durable checkpoint or stable event key so overlap does not repage the same event. A simple `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` window is acceptable only after measured delay proves it safe; otherwise use a reviewed correlation-search framework that tracks event identity.

## Step 4 — Create and understand the detection

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_builtin_administrators_membership_changes`. The base term fixes the deployment index, both qualified Security sources/types, event IDs 4732/4733, and the language-independent group SID. `eval` maps only 4732 to `added` and 4733 to `removed`; it builds display values while preserving every raw SID field. `where` rejects malformed events without action, member SID, or actor SID. The final table keeps the audit identity and sorts for analyst review. There is intentionally no statistical threshold: one audited membership operation is one result.

Alert additions at high severity when no exact approved workflow exists. Removals may be lower severity but remain reviewable, particularly for required recovery/service principals or suspicious add-then-remove sequences. Never label every 4732 as attacker activity. MITRE T1098.007 is applicable because an adversary may add an account to a local or domain group for persistence or privilege; the event alone establishes behavior consistent with that technique, not adversary intent.

The Windows add-on documents 4732/4733 in Change data-model mappings, including `Change.Account_Management` for XML in relevant releases and other Change datasets across releases. Validate tags, event types, and normalized fields in the installed version before building a CIM search. Do not substitute a broad `from datamodel=Change.All_Changes | where count>0`; it loses the exact target SID and can mix unrelated changes.

## Step 5 — Enrich authorization without hiding evidence

Maintain `windows_local_admin_change_approvals.csv` or a governed KV collection. Require exact lowercased stable host identity, member SID, actor SID, action, inclusive `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, ticket, owner, approver, workflow ID, and reason. Validate numeric times, start before expiry, short maximum duration, no duplicate/overlapping records, and no wildcard SID/host. Match after the base result. Preserve `approval_match`, ticket, and lookup revision with the detection.

Use authoritative identity and asset sources to resolve member and actor SIDs, but keep original SIDs. Distinguish users, groups, computers, deleted principals, local SIDs, and domain SIDs. Do not assume `MemberName=-` means an invalid or benign account. Enrich actor logon ID with nearby 4624 or 4648 events only where retention and host identity support it; a correlation miss must not remove the membership event or invent a source workstation.

## Step 6 — Validate controls and semantics

Run the exact `controlTest` variants in an isolated index with fixed event payloads and dispatch times. Assert one output per unique 4732/4733, exact action mapping, target SID filtering, unresolved-member handling, actor preservation, source/type restriction, and raw identity fields. Add tests for localized group names with the same SID, misleading `TargetUserName=Administrators` with the wrong SID, numeric/string EventCode representations, missing actor/member SID, event record ID absent in a qualified classic event, duplicate transport copies, late arrival, and two legitimate rapid add/remove operations.

In a disposable Windows lab, perform one approved add and removal and compare Splunk fields with Event Viewer raw XML at the same time. Confirm the actor is the subject that performed the operation, not the changed member. Confirm one event per member. Test local user, domain user, and domain group members; record when `MemberName` is `-`. Validate current group state separately with a read-only inventory command and restore it. Documentation review alone does not satisfy this runtime gate.

Test notification policy independently: unmatched addition alerts; exact approved addition is marked/suppressed only for delivery; wrong host/member/actor/action, before-start, at-expiry, missing ticket, wildcard, or expired approval does not suppress; removal still records; and source-health findings can never be suppressed by a change approval. Record alert latency, duplicate behavior, and checkpoint recovery after search-head restart.

## Step 7 — Operationalize response and evidence

Alert text should state `Built-in Administrators member <SID> <added|removed> on <host> by <actor SID>`. Include UTC event/index time, target/member/actor names and SIDs, actor logon ID, event record ID, asset owner/tier, approval status, ticket, nearby session evidence, current membership state, and runbook link.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw 4732/4733 XML, target SID, host, event identity, required fields, collection health, and duplicate status.
2. Resolve actor/member SIDs through authoritative identity systems while preserving unresolved values.
3. Confirm current local Administrators membership through an approved read-only endpoint-management or Windows command path.
4. Check the exact change/PAM/build/MDM workflow, approver, execution identity, scope, and expiry.
5. Correlate actor logon, process/PowerShell/endpoint telemetry, remote-management, and policy deployment only where those sources are available; do not infer absent facts.
6. For unauthorized additions, follow incident procedure to contain the account/host and remove access through approved administration. Preserve evidence before remediation.
7. For removals, determine whether access revocation was expected or whether a required service/recovery principal was lost.
8. Confirm post-response current state, paired removal where appropriate, no conflicting policy re-add, alert closure rationale, and retained evidence.

Never automatically remove a member, disable an account, isolate a host, edit Group Policy/MDM, or roll back a change from this search alone. Those actions can interrupt management and recovery access and require accountable approval.

## Step 8 — Troubleshoot and maintain

- **No events after a lab change:** verify effective advanced audit policy, Security channel, provider/event ID, input assignment, Windows Event Collector subscription, forwarder queues, index routing/RBAC, source/type, and time range. Inspect Event Viewer before blaming extraction.
- **Target name matches but SID does not:** trust the raw SID and investigate localization, extraction collision, test data, or a different group. Never broaden to name-only matching.
- **MemberName is `-`:** expected for some local-group changes. Resolve `MemberSid` separately and preserve the hyphen.
- **Actor and member appear reversed:** inspect raw XML and field aliases. Subject is the initiating principal; Member is the changed principal; Target is the group.
- **Duplicate alerts:** identify overlapping subscriptions/forwarders using computer, channel, provider, and record ID. Repair routing and checkpoint notification without collapsing legitimate repeat changes.
- **CIM search differs from raw:** inspect installed add-on version, event types, tags, dataset, field aliases, acceleration range, and source rendering. Keep the Microsoft-field raw search authoritative until parity passes.
- **Add then remove occurs quickly:** retain both events. It may be JIT administration, failed automation, attacker cleanup, or policy conflict; compare workflow and process/session evidence.
- **Dashboard is green for silent hosts:** fix source-health logic; absence is unknown, never compliant state.

Review covered inventory, audit policy, add-on/OS versions, source/type, required fields, delay window, duplicate handling, SID-resolution source, approvals, alert routes, dashboard, and runbook quarterly and after Windows, policy, forwarding, add-on, index, identity, PAM, MDM, or deployment changes. Keep `status=draft` until accountable Windows, security, and Splunk owners execute and sign the complete test matrix.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for anyone being added to or removed from the small list of people who can fully control a Windows computer. Each change shows who made it and whose access changed, so the team can quickly check that it was approved.
